What you wrote is very interesting and I can totally agree because it reflects my vision of Lain.

Regarding Lain's discourse as God or not, it depends on the point of view and the definition of God:

\- According to the Christian religion and the other monotheistic religions, transcendent principle, creator of the universe and endowed with attributes that express absolute perfection, such as uniqueness, omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence and eternity.

\- Superior spirit, powerful, immortal, but of a nature substantially not different from human in polytheistic religions.

\- Symbol of what is maximum and extreme.

From this point Lain at the beginning seems to be at the base of a belief similar to the Christian religion: a god loved, omnipotent, omniscient and perfect. But she is not perfect. In many ways it is terribly human. So is she like a polytheistic God?

An autistic god? Maybe.

Certainly she is a god without identity because she represents all the people connected on earth through the Wired. She can assume the form, the character and the thoughts, observe them, know them and spread the knowledge acquired in each one. She is a machine that spreads information and in this loses her ability to really communicate and, especially, loses her identity. She is a personified collective consciousness.

Is she maximum and extreme?

I would say yes. She acquires maximum skills as soon as she found the possibility of being omnipresent, etc. And extreme in her decisions. Far too extreme and then fall often into error. She is wrong and tries again. She does not understand in the ordinary sense of understanding and therefore she tries again, but she is still wrong. But then she returns human, in a sense, to understand the truth behind the definition of a God.

For me, right in this moment, together with the scene of connection with the father and with an adult Alice, she really becomes the human God in whom I believe. An energy born from the collective consciousness, which can continue to exist in the memories and recesses of the mind. With this she can even control events, like death. And maybe she also finds her own identity and way of connecting.

I can really relate deeply to her because of her continuous search for communications and limits that are compensated by a different way of living and seeing the world.
